title: How to Make People Like You in 90 Seconds or Less
author: Nicholas Boothman
target_audience: Business professionals seeking to improve first impressions
Individuals interested in strengthening social skills
Anyone looking for practical techniques to connect quickly in social or networking situations
core_themes: Rapport-building through verbal and non-verbal communication
Techniques for making authentic connections quickly
The role of body language and attitude in likability
Simple practices to boost charm and approachability
primary_purpose: To equip readers with step-by-step methods for rapidly establishing rapport and creating positive, lasting first impressions with anyone they meet.

structure_format.narrative_style: Practical, concise, and conversational, with a focus on actionable advice and real-life examples
structure_format.organization: Divided into thematic chapters outlining techniques, with step-by-step exercises and summaries
features: Simple models for understanding and practicing rapport

key_concepts_lessons: First impressions are formed rapidly—often in less than two minutes.
The combination of attitude, body language, and verbal cues creates immediate rapport.
The 'Basic Law of Rapport': people like people who are like themselves or who make them feel good.
Mirroring and matching body language fosters connection at a subconscious level.
Active listening and displaying genuine curiosity increase likability.
Being present and aware in every interaction is key to making meaningful connections.
notable_features: Widely used in business, sales, and networking contexts
cultural_historical_context: Released at the turn of the millennium when interest in emotional intelligence, networking, and rapid social connection was rising in the workplace and beyond. The book was part of a wave of practical guides for interpersonal effectiveness.
reception_impact: Popular with business professionals, salespeople, and students for its easy-to-apply advice
Translated into multiple languages and used globally as a training resource
Generally praised for its clarity and actionable steps
Some critics note reliance on formulaic approaches and question depth for more advanced readers
comparable_titles: How to Win Friends and Influence People by Dale Carnegie
The Like Switch by Jack Schafer
How to Talk to Anyone by Leil Lowndes
